claims.text: Controlled oxidation during wear promotes formation of a thin, graded oxide tribolayer on CoCrFeMnNi coatings.
The oxide tribolayer stabilizes the sliding interface.
The oxide tribolayer reduces adhesive wear.
Reducing adhesive wear and micro-plowing enhances the wear resistance of the coating.
The composition of the graded oxide tribolayer is directly influenced by oxygen exposure level.
The thickness of the graded oxide tribolayer is directly influenced by oxygen exposure level.
A thin oxide layer changes the surface energy of the coating.
A thin oxide layer changes the frictional characteristics of the coating.
The oxide film minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact.
An oxide film that is too thick or non-uniform can increase wear.
An optimal oxidation condition exists that provides the best wear performance.
Moderate controlled oxygen exposure should produce a uniform oxide tribolayer.
Moderate controlled oxygen exposure should lower the friction coefficient relative to an inert-argon baseline.
Moderate controlled oxygen exposure should reduce wear volume relative to an inert-argon baseline.
The proposed mechanism should apply at room temperature when oxidation kinetics permit formation of a thin protective film.
Extreme oxygen pressure or temperature may move oxidation kinetics outside the protective-film regime.

contradictions.description: The predicted-outcome field says that an absence of the expected improvement would support the critical role of the tribolayer, whereas the falsification rule says that failure to improve friction and wear under moderate oxygen exposure would falsify the hypothesis.
